props.title: Thieves' Highway

sections.content: Jules Dassin's gritty noir **Thieves' Highway** (1949) revolutionized the crime thriller by taking it out of dark city streets and into California's sun-baked produce markets. Richard Conte stars as Nick Garcos, a returning war veteran seeking revenge against the crooked produce dealer who crippled his father. The film's brutal portrayal of the cutthroat produce transportation business exposed the dark underbelly of post-war American capitalism. Like Dassin's later masterpiece **Night and the City** (1950), it shows how desperation and greed corrupt ordinary people.

sections.content: What sets **Thieves' Highway** apart is its documentary-like attention to the details of trucking and produce markets. Shot on location in San Francisco's wholesale market district, it captures the authentic rhythms and dangers of long-haul trucking in the 1940s. The film shares DNA with Italian Neorealism, particularly **Bitter Rice** (1949), in its focus on working-class struggles and real locations. Dassin's unflinching camera shows every aspect of the trade - from haggling over prices to sabotaged trucks.

The film represents the peak of Dassin's American period, before Hollywood blacklisting forced him to Europe where he made classics like **Rififi** (1955). The noir elements - betrayal, femme fatales, moral ambiguity - feel especially potent when transplanted from shadowy urban settings to the harsh daylight of California highways and loading docks. Lee J. Cobb's performance as the villainous Mike Figlia established a template for noir antagonists who hide their evil behind legitimate business fronts. SUBHEAD: Working Class Noir

sections.content: **Thieves' Highway** pioneered a subgenre of noir focused on blue-collar workers rather than private eyes or gangsters. Films like **The Set-Up** (1949) and **The Breaking Point** (1950) followed its lead in examining how ordinary working men get dragged into criminal enterprises. The film's political undertones - critiquing unfettered capitalism while celebrating worker solidarity - reflect both Dassin's leftist leanings and the progressive spirit that would soon be quashed by McCarthyism.
